nameStory: The yellow jack gets its straightforward name from its golden-yellow coloration that shimmers in the water like a flash of sunlight. The 'jack' part comes from the family name - all members of the Carangidae family are called jacks, likely from their quick, darting movements that reminded early fishermen of the nimble movements of a person named Jack.
description: The yellow jack is a sleek, golden-colored fish that's built for speed with a streamlined body perfect for chasing prey through open water. These impressive fish can grow quite large - up to 3 feet long and weighing over 30 pounds, though most you'll encounter are much smaller. They're predatory fish that hunt other smaller fish, either alone or in small groups around reefs and rocky areas. While they range from Massachusetts to Brazil, they're quite rare visitors to New England waters.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow body that catches light like polished brass, often with silvery highlights along the sides that create an almost metallic sheen

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Torpedo-shaped and laterally compressed (flattened from side to side) with a sleek profile built for fast swimming through open water

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Distinctive forked tail fin and pointed dorsal and anal fins that feel firm and muscular to the touch, with specific ray counts that distinguish it from relatives

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth (opens at the front tip of the head) with a jaw that extends relatively far back compared to similar jacks, reaching past the eye

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach impressive sizes up to 3 feet long, but most encountered are in the 1-2 foot range with a solid, muscular feel when handled

habitat: In New England's waters, yellow jacks are extremely rare visitors typically found around rocky reefs, jetties, and structured areas in deeper coastal waters. They prefer warmer waters and are most likely encountered during the warmest months around offshore structures or near the warmer currents of the Gulf Stream influence.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare in New England waters during spring as water temperatures are still too cold for this warm-water species.
seasonality.summer: Most likely time to encounter a yellow jack in New England waters when ocean temperatures peak, though sightings remain exceptionally rare.
seasonality.fall: Possible but unlikely sightings as water temperatures begin to cool and any visiting individuals move south.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters due to cold temperatures, having migrated to warmer southern waters.

funFact: Despite being called a 'jack,' yellow jacks can live for decades and the largest specimens are thought to be 20+ years old - these golden speedsters are basically the sports cars of the reef with the longevity of a classic automobile!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative the blue runner, but yellow jacks are distinctly more golden-yellow while blue runners are more silvery-blue. The yellow jack's jaw also extends farther back past the eye - remember 'yellow = jaw extends.'
contextualKnowledge: Yellow jacks are also known as 'coolihoo' in some Caribbean areas, a name that sounds almost musical. With only 3 recorded observations in New England waters, spotting one here would be like finding a tropical tourist who took a very wrong turn north.
compareHints: Compared to the more common crevalle jack, yellow jacks have a more golden coloration and longer jaw that extends past the eye. Blue runners are more silvery-blue and smaller overall, while yellow jacks maintain their golden hue and can grow much larger. The jaw length is the key distinguishing feature among all the Atlantic Caranx species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relatives, the Blue Runner has a more elongated body and lacks the crevalle jack's steep forehead profile, while the Yellow Jack (rare in New England) is more golden overall and has a less compressed body shape.

Compared to its close relatives, the blue runner is distinguished by its prominent blue stripe - crevalle jacks lack this blue coloration and have a more golden appearance with a black gill spot, while yellow jacks are, as their name suggests, more yellow overall.
